title: The Hartford's Third-Quarter Core Earnings Slip 6% to $956 Million as Catastrophe Losses Nearly Triple, While a $497 Million Asbestos Gain and a CEO Handover Take the Headlines
summary: The Hartford reported on October 26, 2026 third-quarter core earnings of $956 million ($3.50 a share), down 6%, as catastrophe losses rose to $198 million from $70 million, while net income rose 23% to $1.317 billion on a $497 million gain from commuting its asbestos and environmental reinsurance cover, and Mo Tooker will succeed Chris Swift as CEO on March 1.
description:
The Hartford Insurance Group reported its third-quarter 2026 results on October 26, 2026, in an earnings news release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission as an exhibit to a Form 8-K. The headline figures point in two directions, and understanding why requires separating the company's measure of underlying profit from its reported net income. Core earnings, which exclude items such as realised investment gains and losses, certain reserve actions and discontinued operations, were $956 million, or $3.50 per diluted share. That was down 6 per cent in dollars from the third quarter of 2025 and down 3 per cent per share, from $3.59, which is consistent with a lower share count. Net income available to common stockholders, by contrast, rose 23 per cent to $1.317 billion, or $4.82 per diluted share, from $3.77. Income from continuing operations was $1.262 billion, or $4.60 per share, up 24 per cent. On a trailing twelve-month basis, the net income return on equity was 25.0 per cent and the core earnings return on equity was 17.9 per cent.

The gap between the two measures comes mostly from reserves and discontinued operations. The company reported net favorable prior-year reserve development of $594 million before tax, of which $497 million was a gain from commuting its asbestos and environmental adverse development cover. An adverse development cover is a reinsurance contract that pays if losses on old claims turn out worse than reserved; commuting such a contract means settling it early for a lump sum. Excluding that gain, core favorable development was $97 million, roughly flat against $95 million a year earlier, so the routine pattern of small reserve releases continued. The release also notes that Hartford Funds, whose sale was agreed on June 3, 2026, is reported as discontinued operations and contributed $61 million to net income but is excluded from core earnings.

Weather explains the decline in core earnings. Property and casualty current accident year catastrophe losses were $198 million before tax, up from $70 million, which is roughly 2.8 times the earlier amount on simple division. Business Insurance bore $106 million, up from $39 million, and Personal Insurance $92 million, up from $31 million. The effect shows in the combined ratios, which measure claims and expenses as a share of premium. Business Insurance reported a combined ratio of 91.3 against 88.8, and an underlying combined ratio, which strips out catastrophes and prior-year development, of 90.1 against 89.4. Personal Insurance reported 93.2 against 88.7, but its underlying combined ratio improved to 87.1 from 90.0. The difference between 93.2 and 87.1 is about six points, which is the combined effect of catastrophes and reserve movements on that book; this is an arithmetic observation, not a figure from the release. In plain terms, personal lines' underlying business improved even as weather worsened the reported result.

Premium trends show a company growing where it wants to and shrinking where it chooses to. Written premiums in Business Insurance, the commercial lines segment, grew 6 per cent to $3.8 billion. Personal Insurance written premiums fell 4 per cent to $950 million. Group Benefits, the employee benefits business, reported fully insured ongoing premiums up 4 per cent to $1.662 billion. The release does not explain the personal lines decline, and the figures alone cannot show whether it reflects deliberate underwriting or customer losses. In Group Benefits the loss ratio rose to 74.9 from 70.1, while the expense ratio improved to 25.4 from 26.7, so the segment's margin tightened slightly on claims.

Investment income remained a source of strength. Net investment income was $850 million, up 13 per cent from $755 million. Excluding limited partnerships, which are private fund interests whose returns are reported with a lag and vary more, it was $694 million, up 5 per cent. Limited partnership income was $156 million against $91 million, a yield of 10.2 per cent against 6.7 per cent. The annualised investment yield was 5.1 per cent against 4.8 per cent. Against that, net realised losses were $116 million, up from $17 million. Together these figures show that a notable part of the improvement in total investment income came from the partnership line, which is less predictable than interest on bonds.

On capital, book value per diluted share was $68.31, up 7 per cent from a year earlier and up 3.0 per cent from December 31, 2025. Excluding accumulated other comprehensive income, which captures unrealised gains and losses on bonds, it was $82.47, up 16 per cent. The company returned $638 million to stockholders in the quarter: $475 million in share repurchases and $163 million in common dividends. It raised its quarterly common dividend by 12 per cent to $0.67 per share, payable on January 5, 2027.

The release also contains a leadership change. Mo Tooker will succeed Chris Swift as chief executive on March 1, and Swift will become executive chair. Swift described the quarter as another strong result in an increasingly competitive market, which is the phrase to watch: competitive markets usually mean softer commercial pricing and more pressure on margins, which is consistent with the rise in the Business Insurance underlying ratio of 0.7 points. The release does not give commercial pricing figures, nor nine-month results, so the full-year picture is not covered here.

Several cautions apply. The 23 per cent rise in net income should not be read as a rise in underlying profitability, because the largest single contributor was a one-time commutation gain. The catastrophe figure of $198 million is for the quarter only and covers events the company defines as catastrophes, so it is not comparable with the monthly series that other insurers publish. And the company's statements about competition are general; the release does not quantify them. What to watch next is the pace of commercial rate changes, the effect of the Hartford Funds sale on capital deployment, and whether personal lines premiums stabilise after the 4 per cent fall.
source_name: The Hartford Form 8-K earnings news release (October 26, 2026)

key_points: Third-quarter 2026 core earnings were $956 million, or $3.50 per diluted share, down 6% in dollars and 3% per share from $3.59, while net income available to common stockholders rose 23% to $1.317 billion ($4.82 per share).

Property and casualty current accident year catastrophe losses were $198 million against $70 million a year earlier, lifting the Business Insurance combined ratio to 91.3 from 88.8 and the Personal Insurance combined ratio to 93.2 from 88.7.

Net favorable prior-year reserve development was $594 million, including a $497 million gain from commuting the asbestos and environmental adverse development cover; core favorable development was $97 million, roughly flat on $95 million.

Written premiums grew 6% to $3.8 billion in Business Insurance and 4% to $1.662 billion in Group Benefits but fell 4% to $950 million in Personal Insurance, while net investment income rose 13% to $850 million.

The Hartford returned $638 million to stockholders in the quarter, raised its quarterly dividend 12% to $0.67 per share, and announced that Mo Tooker will succeed Chris Swift as chief executive on March 1, with Swift becoming executive chair.
why_it_matters: The Hartford's quarter shows how much of an insurer's headline profit can come from items that are not recurring: a one-time asbestos commutation gain lifted net income, while the underlying picture, measured by core earnings, softened as weather losses rose. The company's own words, an increasingly competitive market, match what other commercial insurers report, so the results are a useful read on where the US pricing cycle stands.

title: Cincinnati Financial's Third-Quarter Operating Income Holds at $443 Million Even as Catastrophe Losses Add 7 Points to the Combined Ratio, and Net Income Falls 59% on Missing Equity Gains
summary: Cincinnati Financial reported on October 26, 2026 third-quarter non-GAAP operating income of $443 million ($2.86 a share) against $449 million, a property casualty combined ratio of 90.9% that was 2.7 points worse as catastrophe losses added 7.0 points, and net income of $459 million versus $1.122 billion because last year's quarter included about $855 million of pre-tax equity gains.
description:
Cincinnati Financial Corporation, the Ohio-based property casualty insurer that sells through independent agents, reported its third-quarter 2026 results on October 26, 2026. In the earnings release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, net income was $459 million, or $2.96 per share, compared with $1.122 billion, or $7.11 per share, in the third quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP operating income, which excludes investment gains and losses, was $443 million, or $2.86 per share, against $449 million, or $2.85 per share. The two numbers moved in very different ways for a reason that the release spells out, and it is the most important thing to understand about the quarter.

The $663 million fall in net income was mainly a $657 million drop, after tax, in net investment gains. Cincinnati holds a large portfolio of equity securities, and under accounting rules the change in their market value flows through net income. The third quarter of 2025 included about $855 million of pre-tax unrealised gains on equity securities that the company still held, whereas the comparable gain in the third quarter of 2026 was $1 million. Lower underwriting profit, down $41 million, was partly offset by $24 million more investment income. Put simply, the business that sells insurance earned roughly what it earned a year ago; the large difference in net income reflects stock market valuation changes. For nine months, net income was $1.988 billion, or $12.75 per share, up from $1.717 billion, and operating income was $997 million, or $6.39 per share, compared with $723 million, or $4.58, a rise of 38 per cent in dollars.

Weather is the main change in underwriting. The property casualty combined ratio, claims and expenses as a share of earned premium, was 90.9 per cent, up 2.7 points from 88.2 per cent. Current accident year catastrophe losses were 10.8 per cent of consolidated earned premiums against 4.4 per cent, which is the 7.0-point increase the company cites; applied to consolidated earned premiums of $2.605 billion, that is roughly $281 million, a figure derived here by arithmetic and not stated in the release. Favorable prior-year reserve development helped: $94 million, or 3.6 points, against $22 million, or 0.9 points. For nine months the combined ratio was 95.8 per cent, an improvement of 2.6 points from 98.4 per cent, with catastrophe losses 1.3 points lower than in the first nine months of 2025. Chief executive Stephen Spray said the 95.8 per cent is comfortably within the company's long-term target of 92 per cent to 98 per cent.

The segment results show where the quarter's margin came from. Commercial lines posted a combined ratio of 92.8 per cent with net written premiums of about $1.199 billion, essentially flat on $1.198 billion, up less than 1 per cent. Personal lines had a combined ratio of 90.3 per cent with net written premiums up 1 per cent to $957 million from $951 million. Excess and surplus lines, a smaller segment that writes hard-to-place risks, posted 89.4 per cent against 89.8 per cent, with net written premiums up 5 per cent to $184 million, and for the nine months a combined ratio of 89.7 per cent and written premiums up 7 per cent to $585 million. Other results, which include the company's reinsurance and Lloyd's operations, were an underwriting profit of $39 million against $64 million, with net written premiums of $210 million against $169 million; for nine months, Cincinnati Specialty Underwriters grew 7 per cent, Cincinnati Global 13 per cent and Cincinnati Re 11 per cent. The release does not report the results of those units separately.

Pricing data from the agency channel are the closest indicator of where the market is heading. Consolidated agency renewal written premiums rose 3 per cent to $2.095 billion from $2.037 billion. Commercial renewal premiums rose 1 per cent, with low-single-digit renewal pricing increases. Personal lines renewal premiums rose 5 per cent, with rate increases near the low end of the high-single-digit range. Excess and surplus renewal premiums rose 3 per cent with low-single-digit price increases. These are modest numbers compared with the double-digit increases of recent years, and they fit the picture of a commercial market in which price increases are fading while claims costs are not.

Investment income remained a bright spot. Pretax investment income was $325 million, up 10 per cent from $295 million, and for nine months $962 million, up 12 per cent. Consolidated earned premiums were $2.690 billion, up 5 per cent, and $7.929 billion for nine months, up 7 per cent. The life insurance subsidiary earned $31 million, up 11 per cent, and $87 million for nine months, up 16 per cent. The property casualty segment's net written premiums were $2.550 billion, up 2 per cent, and $8.043 billion for nine months, up 4 per cent.

The balance sheet and capital figures reflect the equity swing. Book value per share was $105.42 at September 30, 2026, up 7 per cent from $98.76 a year earlier. The value creation ratio, the company's measure of growth in book value plus dividends, was negative 2.1 per cent for the quarter against 8.9 per cent, and 5.8 per cent for nine months against 13.8 per cent. The board declared a quarterly dividend of $0.94 per share, up 8 per cent from $0.87, and $2.82 for nine months, up 8 per cent. The release does not discuss share repurchases directly, but treasury stock rose from $2.732 billion at the end of 2025 to $3.132 billion at the end of September, and diluted weighted average shares fell to 155.1 million from 157.8 million, which indicates continued buybacks.

For readers comparing insurers, the lesson is to look at operating income and the combined ratio rather than net income when stock markets are volatile. Cincinnati's own words, that its overall combined ratio of 90.9 per cent reflects continued efforts in pricing segmentation and that its insurance operations continued to lead the way, point to underwriting as the engine of the quarter. What to watch is whether catastrophe activity in the fourth quarter affects the full-year ratio, how renewal pricing evolves as the commercial market softens, and whether equity valuation changes continue to dominate reported earnings.
image_alt: Commercial and residential buildings representing property and casualty insurance (illustrative)
key_points: Third-quarter 2026 net income was $459 million ($2.96 a share) against $1.122 billion ($7.11), while non-GAAP operating income was $443 million ($2.86) against $449 million ($2.85).

The property casualty combined ratio was 90.9%, 2.7 points higher than 88.2%, as catastrophe losses added 7.0 points and favorable prior-year reserve development of $94 million (3.6 points) offset part of the increase.

Nine-month operating income rose to $997 million ($6.39 a share) from $723 million, and the nine-month combined ratio improved to 95.8% from 98.4%, within the company's long-term target range of 92% to 98%.

Consolidated earned premiums rose 5% to $2.690 billion and pretax investment income rose 10% to $325 million, while agency renewal premiums rose 3%, with personal lines up 5% on rate increases near the low end of the high-single-digit range.
Book value per share was $105.42, up 7% from a year earlier, the quarterly dividend was raised 8% to $0.94, and the value creation ratio was negative 2.1% for the quarter against 8.9% a year earlier.
why_it_matters: Cincinnati's quarter is a clean illustration of why net income can mislead: an accounting swing in equity valuations moved net income by hundreds of millions of dollars, while operating income barely changed. Underneath, the insurer absorbed a 7-point catastrophe hit and still posted a combined ratio under 91%, which is a useful benchmark for how well-run regional commercial and personal lines writers are coping with heavier weather.

title: Storm Austen Leaves More Than 280,000 Customers Without Power in Northwest France With 100 mph Gusts, but Cotality Expects Modest, Widely Spread Insured Losses
summary: Storm Austen crossed southern Britain and northern France on October 23, 2026 with gusts of 100 mph at Pointe du Raz, cutting power to more than 280,000 French customers; Cotality expects relatively modest property damage spread across smaller claims, and French guidance explains how storm cover and the CatNat scheme apply.
description:
Storm Austen, the first named storm of the 2026-27 European winter season, moved across southern Britain and northern France on Friday, October 23, 2026, according to Cotality's Hazard HQ service. The UK Met Office named it on Tuesday, October 20, and by Friday it was crossing the English Channel with a central pressure of around 974 hectopascals, reaching the Low Countries by late morning. Cotality reported peak gusts of 100 mph, or about 161 km/h, at Pointe du Raz in Finistère, and 93 mph at the Île de Groix, both in France. In the United Kingdom the strongest gusts were 76 mph at St. Mary's Airport on the Isles of Scilly, 74 mph at Aberporth in Wales and 71 mph at Culdrose in Cornwall. Météo-France had issued orange wind warnings for more than 20 departments, and the French consumer site Meilleurtaux counted 23 departments under orange alert that morning without naming them. In Britain, the Met Office issued an amber wind warning for Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of west Devon, with yellow warnings across much of England and Wales.

The disruption was widespread. Cotality reported that more than 280,000 customers lost power in northwest France, more than 9,000 homes in Cornwall and Devon lost supply, and about 3,000 customers were affected in Ireland. In France three bridges in Normandy were closed and rail services were disrupted. In the United Kingdom, flights and trains were cancelled, schools in the south-west closed, fallen trees blocked roads in Cornwall and part of Brighton's West Pier collapsed. Trees fell in Waterford and Cork in Ireland, and roads flooded in north Staffordshire, where the Environment Agency had flood warnings in several regions. Storm Boelo followed: the Met Office issued an amber warning for much of Scotland, Northumberland, Cumbria and parts of Northern Ireland from 9 p.m. on Saturday, October 24 to 9 p.m. on Sunday, October 25, with gusts of 60 to 70 mph forecast and up to 80 mph on exposed coasts, and Met Éireann issued orange warnings for several western counties.

The most relevant question for the insurance industry is how large the losses will be, and the answer so far is that nobody has published a number. Cotality's page contains no dollar or pound estimate. Its senior weather scientist, Mark Dixon, said the company expects property damage to be relatively modest, spread across smaller claims rather than catastrophic, and that Austen's pattern, fallen trees, roof and fence damage and outages, is that of a typical early-season windstorm and not of large structural losses. He said claims are likely to be most concentrated in Brittany and Normandy, and added that windstorms remain a risk and have historically caused very large losses, with further claims expected over the weekend because of Storm Boelo.

For policyholders in France, Meilleurtaux set out how cover works in a guide published on the day of the storm. Home insurance policies usually include storm cover, known as garantie tempête. Insurers may require proof that winds were abnormally strong; according to ANIL, the national housing information agency quoted in the guide, they often ask for a certificate from a nearby weather station, or evidence that the wind damaged other well-built buildings within 5 kilometres. The separate natural disaster scheme, known as CatNat, applies only if winds averaged at least 145 km/h over ten minutes or reached 215 km/h in gusts. As a simple comparison, Austen's peak gust of about 161 km/h at Pointe du Raz is below the 215 km/h gust threshold, but gusts and ten-minute averages are different measures, and whether any commune qualifies for CatNat is a decision for the authorities and is not stated in the reports.

The claims process has set deadlines. The guide says that damage should generally be declared within five days of discovery, extended to 30 days if a ministerial order recognises the commune as a natural disaster zone. Tenants should tell their landlord about structural damage, since the owner makes that claim, and make their own claim for belongings with their own insurer. Examples of damage that France Assureurs lists as covered include fallen trees, roof damage or removal, furniture damaged by rain after a roof is damaged, and some flooding from related episodes. Deductibles under storm cover vary by contract and are usually below 380 euros, averaging 150 to 200 euros, while the CatNat deductible is 380 euros. Payouts depend on the contract's limits, ceiling and depreciation.

Exclusions and gaps are worth knowing. Vehicles fall under motor policies, not home insurance. Broken glass requires the optional glass breakage guarantee. Garden items such as fences, verandas and swimming pools are not included in every policy, and undeclared additions, such as a new garden shed, may not be covered. The guide does not give the number of claims, departmental lists or total insured losses, and the Cotality page does not either, so this article cannot provide them.

Context matters, too. Austen arrived after a month in which French insurers were dealing with the aftermath of the October 17 riots, which Morningstar DBRS estimated could cost insurers up to 1.2 billion euros, and a summer of record wildfire claims. A storm that produces many small claims adds to the workload of loss adjusters and call centres, even if the financial effect is modest. In the United Kingdom, where the storm caused outages, travel disruption and the collapse of part of a pier, typical home insurance policies cover storm damage to buildings and contents, subject to excesses, but no UK loss figures were given in the reports reviewed.

What to watch is whether Météo-France or the authorities recognise any commune under CatNat, whether modelers such as Cotality or PERILS publish loss estimates after the follow-on Storm Boelo, and whether the pattern of early storms continues into the winter. For households, the immediate advice is to photograph damage, make safe, and file the claim within the deadline.
image_alt: Storm-damaged homes after a severe weather event (illustrative)
key_points: Storm Austen, named by the UK Met Office on October 20 as the first name on the 2026-27 list, crossed southern Britain and northern France on October 23 with a central pressure of around 974 hPa.
Peak gusts included 100 mph at Pointe du Raz and 93 mph at the Île de Groix in France, 76 mph at St. Mary's in the Isles of Scilly, and 74 mph at Aberporth in Wales.

More than 280,000 customers lost power in northwest France, over 9,000 homes in Cornwall and Devon and about 3,000 customers in Ireland; three Normandy bridges closed and rail services were disrupted.

Cotality's Mark Dixon said the company expects property damage to be relatively modest, spread across smaller claims, rather than catastrophic, with claims most concentrated in Brittany and Normandy; no loss estimate has been published.

French home insurance usually includes storm cover (garantie tempête), the CatNat natural disaster scheme applies only above wind thresholds of 145 km/h averaged over ten minutes or 215 km/h gusts, and claims should generally be filed within five days of discovering damage.
why_it_matters: Windstorms are the largest European weather peril for insurers, but not every named storm is a major loss event. Austen's early-season track and wind speeds point to many small claims for fallen trees, roofs and fences rather than structural destruction, which tests insurers' claims handling more than their balance sheets. For households, the practical value lies in knowing which cover responds and how quickly to file.

title: OSFI Tells Canadian P&C and Mortgage Insurers Q4 Filings Stay the Same, Then IFRS 18 Returns Start in Q1 2027, and the Final 2027 MICAT Cuts the Low-Rise Housing Risk Weight to 130%
summary: OSFI letters dated October 22, 2026 confirm that Q4 2026 returns for federally regulated property and casualty and mortgage insurers are unchanged, that updated IFRS 18 returns start in Q1 2027 for December year-end companies and November 1, 2027 for October year-end companies, and that the final 2027 MICAT guideline lowers the base risk weight for low-rise multi-unit construction from 150% to 130% from January 1, 2027.
description:
Canada's federal financial regulator has sent two letters to the insurers it supervises that, taken together, set the reporting calendar for the next year. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, known as OSFI, wrote on October 22, 2026 to the chief executives and chief agents of federally regulated property and casualty insurers and Canadian branches of foreign insurers, and separately to mortgage insurers. Insurance Business Canada reported both letters on October 23, 2026. The core message in each is that the fourth quarter of 2026 will be a quiet one, in the sense that no changes are made to the forms insurers file, followed by a larger change in 2027 when the reporting standard IFRS 18 begins to apply.

For property and casualty insurers, the letter covers OSFI's forms and those of the Canadian Council of Insurance Regulators for 2026-27. The Q4 2026 returns that stay as they are include PC1, the core financial quarterly return; PC2 and PC3, the supervisory quarterly and annual returns; and PCPROV, the provincial return. From Q1 2027, all four are updated for IFRS 18. OSFI has already posted the updated returns, instructions and supporting documents on its website, and a summary of changes is in Section VI of the instructions. The PC4 return, which covers the quarterly Minimum Capital Test and the Branch Adequacy of Assets Test, is not changing for Q4 2026 or for Q1 2027. Validation rule updates will be posted in OSFI's regulatory reporting system when they are available, so insurers cannot yet test every check against the new forms.

IFRS 18 is the accounting standard that replaces IAS 1 for annual reporting periods starting on or after January 1, 2027. According to OSFI, as summarised in the coverage, it sorts the profit or loss statement into operating, investing and financing categories. The mortgage insurer article adds that the standard changes how results are presented and disclosed, not how assets or liabilities are measured. That distinction matters: the amount of capital an insurer holds, its reserves and its reported claims do not change because of IFRS 18, but the layout of its income statement does, and so do the totals that appear on regulatory returns. OSFI says its supervisory analysis will not change materially. The coverage does not describe the line-by-line changes, which are in the instructions on OSFI's website.

Timing depends on the financial year end. Companies with a December year end begin filing the IFRS 18 versions in Q1 2027. Those with an October year end stay on the current returns through 2026-27 and switch for the Q1 2027-28 filing period, using the 2026 version of PC4 for Q1 2026-27. For mortgage insurers, the letter says the updated returns take effect on January 1, 2027 for December 31 year-end companies and on November 1, 2027 for October 31 year-end companies. The article notes that, during parts of 2027, insurers may therefore be filing under different layouts depending on their year end, which creates a coordination task for groups with subsidiaries that have different year ends. Calendar-year insurers close 2026 on the old layouts and have one quarter to dry-run the new returns before they are due.

The mortgage insurers' letter has a few additional elements. It is signed by OSFI's chief data officer, Andrew Miller, and says the Q4 2026 filings stay on current forms. The four regular returns that change from Q1 2027 because of IFRS 18 are MI3, the core financial quarterly return; MI4 and MI5, the supervisory quarterly and annual returns; and MIPROV, the provincial return. The MICAT capital return and its filing instructions are also changing, although the letter, as reported, does not say what changes inside the return. Insurance Business reported in September that OSFI had finalised the IFRS 18 return templates.

The change with a direct effect on capital concerns the final 2027 MICAT guideline, which is the capital framework for mortgage insurers. According to the article, it adds a category for low-rise multi-unit residential construction, defined as projects of under seven storeys and 200 units, and lowers the base risk weight from 150 per cent to 130 per cent. High-rise projects stay at 150 per cent, and the change takes effect on January 1, 2027. A risk weight sets how much capital an insurer must hold per dollar of exposure, so, as a simple illustration, a $100 million exposure carrying a 150 per cent weight counts as $150 million of risk-weighted assets, while at 130 per cent it counts as $130 million. The coverage does not state the size of the exposures to which the new category would apply, so the aggregate effect on mortgage insurers' capital is not known from these reports.

For insurers, the practical tasks are clear. Reporting teams should plan the switch now, keep current forms for Q4 2026, and use the IFRS 18 versions from the start date that matches their year end. Questions go to the company's lead supervisor at OSFI or to the returns administration team for help completing or filing. Brokers and investors are less directly affected, although analysts comparing insurers' results across 2027 will need to be aware that the presentation of the income statement is changing and that the first comparable periods will carry both layouts.

What to watch is the posting of validation rules, any further guidance from OSFI on the presentation of insurance contract results under IFRS 18, and the way mortgage insurers describe the effect of the 130 per cent risk weight in their capital disclosures. Regulatory change is often incremental, and these letters confirm the sequence: a quiet quarter, then new returns, with the capital effects flowing mainly through the MICAT guideline.
source_name: Insurance Business Canada (October 23, 2026), reporting OSFI letters dated October 22, 2026
image_alt: Financial documents and charts representing regulatory capital rules (illustrative)
key_points: OSFI's October 22, 2026 letter to property and casualty insurers says the PC1, PC2, PC3 and PCPROV returns are unchanged for Q4 2026 and are updated for IFRS 18 from Q1 2027, while the PC4 capital return has no changes for Q4 2026 or Q1 2027.
A parallel letter to mortgage insurers, signed by OSFI chief data officer Andrew Miller, says the MI3, MI4, MI5 and MIPROV returns and the MICAT capital return change from Q1 2027.

IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 for annual periods starting on or after January 1, 2027 and sorts the profit or loss statement into operating, investing and financing categories; OSFI says its supervisory analysis will not change materially.
December 31 year-end companies file the updated returns from January 1, 2027, while October 31 year-end companies move on November 1, 2027, so insurers will briefly file under different layouts.

The final 2027 MICAT guideline adds a category for low-rise multi-unit residential construction of under seven storeys and 200 units, cutting the base risk weight from 150% to 130% from January 1, 2027, while high-rise projects stay at 150%.
why_it_matters: Regulatory reporting changes rarely make headlines, but they determine how insurers' finance teams spend the next several months and how supervisors will read their numbers. The IFRS 18 switch changes presentation, not measurement, so capital positions should not move because of it, while the MICAT change directly affects the capital that mortgage insurers must hold against certain construction loans.

title: Super Typhoon Champi Passes East of Taiwan With One Dead and Hundreds Hurt, Then Weakens Toward Japan's Kyushu as No Insured Loss Estimates Emerge
summary: Typhoon Champi, the strongest storm of 2026 with peak winds of 296 km/h, passed about 150 km east of Taiwan, killing one person and injuring hundreds, before weakening and heading toward Japan's Kyushu; no insured loss estimates have been published.
description:
Typhoon Champi has become the strongest storm of the 2026 Pacific season, and its first days of impact are now clear enough to describe, even though the cost to insurers is not. Khaleej Times reported on October 21, 2026 that the storm reached peak sustained winds of 296 kilometres per hour, equal to Category 5 strength, making it the fifth super typhoon of the year and the strongest so far. By the time it reached the seas near Taiwan it had weakened, and the centre passed about 150 kilometres to the east of the island, which spared Taiwan a direct landfall but not heavy rain, wind and flooding.

Al Jazeera reported on October 23 that Champi had hit Taiwan, with one person killed and hundreds injured; its headline and metadata referred to 350 injuries. Reuters, in a report carried by The Star on October 24, gave 527 injuries. The difference probably reflects different reporting times as the number of people treated rose, but the sources do not explain it, so the figures should be treated as provisional. The same report said that more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity at one point, according to the state utility Taipower, and Al Jazeera noted that about 56,000 were still without power on Saturday.

Rain was the most serious hazard on the island. Yilan County on the north-east coast received more than 400 millimetres of rain on Friday and about 650 millimetres since Thursday, and forecasters expected as much as 900 millimetres in total. More than 5,000 people were evacuated, and offices and schools were closed for a second day. Air travel was disrupted: Reuters reported between 242 and 259 flights cancelled on the following day, compared with nearly 1,000 cancellations on Friday, so schedules were beginning to recover as the storm moved away.

Japan and China felt the system as well. In Okinawa, two people were injured and about 8,400 households lost power on Friday. In Shanghai, tens of thousands of people were reported evacuated as a precaution. By October 25, Champi had been downgraded to a tropical storm and was forecast to reach Kyushu, Japan's south-western main island, as an extratropical cyclone, a stage at which a storm has lost the warm core of a typhoon but can still bring strong wind and heavy rain. The Star described it as the 30th typhoon of the year in the Pacific.

For insurers, the useful point is what has not been reported. None of the articles gives an estimate of insured losses, and InsuranceAsia News covered the storm behind a subscription wall on October 25, so its estimate, if any, is not available here. Catastrophe modelling firms and Japanese and Taiwanese insurers usually publish early loss ranges only after the storm has passed and surveys begin. For a storm that did not make a direct landfall on Taiwan, a fast-moving passage near Okinawa and a weakening approach to Kyushu, the main insured exposures would be wind and water damage to buildings, vehicles and business interruption in the areas that flooded. Without published claims data, any figure would be speculation.

Context from the weather agencies explains why the season is attracting attention. According to Khaleej Times, the World Meteorological Organization has said that the El Nino climate pattern could be unprecedented, with a peak expected in December. El Nino typically shifts the area where Pacific storms form and can increase the strength of those that develop, although it does not by itself determine where any storm lands. The reports describe the season as active, with Champi the 30th typhoon and the fifth to reach super typhoon intensity.

What to watch next is the path across Kyushu and the weather agencies' final classification of the storm, the first loss estimates from catastrophe modellers and regional insurers, and whether Taiwan's electricity company restores service to the remaining households quickly. A landfall in a populated part of Kyushu would be the first real test of how much damage the weakened system can still do. For readers with property or business interruption insurance in the region, the practical steps are to photograph damage before repairs, notify the insurer promptly and keep receipts for emergency costs.

The scale comparison is worth keeping in mind. A Category 5 storm at sea is not the same as a Category 5 landfall, and the winds that affected people in Taiwan were far below the 296 km/h peak because the centre stayed offshore and the storm had weakened. That is why the main harm in Taiwan came from rain, flooding and power outages rather than structural wind damage. The same logic applies to Japan: what matters for Kyushu is not the peak reached days earlier but the strength, speed and rainfall of the system when it arrives, and the reports describe it as already weakened.

Utilities and transport are the other areas to follow. Power restoration in Taiwan, flight schedules and the reopening of offices and schools will show how quickly normal activity returns, and business interruption claims usually depend on how long operations were halted. Because the storm's centre stayed offshore, these indirect effects may turn out to be larger than direct property damage, but that is an assessment for insurers and modellers to publish once data are available, not a conclusion that the current reports support.
source_name: Al Jazeera (October 23, 2026), Reuters via The Star (October 24, 2026) and Khaleej Times (October 21, 2026)
image_alt: Storm clouds over a coastline representing a typhoon (illustrative)
key_points: Typhoon Champi reached peak sustained winds of 296 km/h, Category 5 strength, the fifth super typhoon of 2026 and the strongest of the year, according to Khaleej Times.
The centre passed about 150 km east of Taiwan, where Reuters reported one death and 527 injuries; Al Jazeera's headline cites hundreds of injuries, so early casualty figures differ between outlets.
More than 167,000 Taiwanese homes lost power at one point and about 56,000 were still without it on Saturday, while 242 to 259 flights were cancelled compared with nearly 1,000 the day before.
Yilan received more than 400 mm of rain in a day and 650 mm since Thursday, with up to 900 mm forecast, and more than 5,000 people were evacuated.
No insurer or catastrophe modeller has published an insured loss estimate, so the storm's cost to the industry is unknown as it moves toward Kyushu as a weaker system.
why_it_matters: Typhoon damage in Taiwan, Japan and China often takes weeks to turn into insured loss figures, and the first headlines on casualties and outages are not a guide to insurance cost. Champi is also a reminder that the 2026 Pacific season is active, with the World Meteorological Organization warning that El Nino could be unusually strong.

title: Suncorp's FY26 Annual Review: A$1.03bn Profit, 18 Natural Hazard Events and an A$254m Allowance Overrun, With a 52c Final Dividend and Up to A$250m More Buy-Back Planned
summary: Suncorp's FY26 annual review reports net profit after tax of A$1,027 million, 18 declared natural hazard events that exceeded the allowance by A$254 million, a 52 cent final dividend and up to A$250 million of further buy-backs, while a regulator review of insurers' claims handling continues in the background.
description:
Suncorp Group's annual review for the financial year ended June 30, 2026, published on its website in August, gives a more complete account of the year than the headline results alone. The CEO and Chairman messages describe a profitable year driven by strong underlying performance, a heavy run of natural hazards and a decision to return surplus capital to shareholders. The picture is also a reminder that results and customer outcomes are measured separately, and the review addresses both.

The main figures are as follows. Net profit after tax was A$1,027 million and cash earnings were A$1,042 million. Underlying earnings rose 4.5 per cent, gross written premium grew 2.7 per cent, and the underlying insurance trading ratio was 11.8 per cent, inside Suncorp's target range of 10 to 12 per cent. The underlying ratio is the measure the company uses for insurance profitability after removing the effect of natural hazard costs that differ from its allowance and some other items. A figure inside the range means the core insurance business performed as planned, even though hazards were costly.

Natural hazards were the main pressure on the year. The company had 18 declared natural hazard events, which led to more than 120,000 claims. The review states that natural hazard claims cost approximately A$2 billion out of total claims spending of about A$10 billion across the group, and that the cost exceeded Suncorp's natural hazard allowance by A$254 million. In other words, about one dollar in five of claims spending went on weather events, and the overrun against budget was meaningful. An allowance is the amount an insurer budgets for such events in a year, so exceeding it reduces earnings relative to plan. Reinsurance and the strength of the underlying result absorbed much of the difference.

Reinsurance changed during the year. The review says a multi-year aggregate reinsurance cover took effect on June 30, 2026. An aggregate cover pays when the accumulated cost of many events passes a threshold, which can protect against the frequency of smaller events as well as one large catastrophe. The reports reviewed here do not give the cover's size, price or attachment point, so its financial effect cannot be quantified from them. Suncorp also reported investment yields of around 5 per cent, which supported earnings as insurers earn income on the premiums they hold before claims are paid.

Shareholders benefited. The final dividend is 52 cents per share, fully franked, taking the full-year dividend to 69 cents, which represents a payout of 70.5 per cent of cash earnings. A special dividend of 10 cents was also announced. The A$400 million on-market buy-back was completed, and the company intends to buy back up to A$250 million more in FY27. Returning capital in this way shows that the board considers the balance sheet to be comfortably above its requirements after the heavy natural hazard year, although the review does not set out the capital figures behind that judgment.

Operations and customer measures are covered as well. The review reports more than 20 generative AI initiatives, an increase in the customer net promoter score to +11.7 from +9.1, and continued work on service. These are company-reported measures, and net promoter score is a survey-based indicator, so they should be read as direction rather than as a verdict on how claims are handled in practice.

Governance changes are also described. Chair Duncan West wrote that chief executive Steve Johnston took medical leave during the year and that chief financial officer Jeremy Robson acted as chief executive in the interim. Directors Sally Herman and Simon Machell are retiring at the annual general meeting, and Yen Saw is joining the board.

The review has to be read alongside the regulatory context. On July 22, 2026, Insurance Business Australia reported that home claims handling failures had put Suncorp in the regulator's crosshairs. That article described an Australian Securities and Investments Commission review of seven insurers' claims action plans between August 2024 and April 2025, which found weak oversight of independent experts used in claims. It also cited a case involving a homeowner, Balzan, in which Suncorp offered A$6,300, and said that Suncorp had 1,968 home and contents complaints at the Australian Financial Complaints Authority in 2024-25. Industry-wide code breaches were reported at 70,325, an increase of 20.5 per cent. The coverage did not report a penalty against Suncorp. These points do not contradict the financial results, but they show that the regulator's attention is on how claims are handled, a topic the annual review addresses through its customer measures.

For customers and brokers, the practical takeaway is that Australia's largest insurers are still paying for severe weather while earning returns, and that scrutiny of claims practices is likely to continue. For investors, the main questions are how the natural hazard allowance is set for FY27, how the new aggregate reinsurance cover performs, and whether the planned buy-back proceeds. Customers who disagree with a claim outcome can use the insurer's internal dispute process and then the Australian Financial Complaints Authority.
source_name: Suncorp Group Annual Review FY26 (CEO and Chairman messages, published August 2026) and Insurance Business Australia
image_alt: Suburban houses representing Australian home insurance (illustrative)
key_points: Suncorp reported FY26 net profit after tax of A$1,027 million and cash earnings of A$1,042 million, with underlying earnings up 4.5% and an underlying insurance trading ratio of 11.8% against a 10% to 12% target.

The group had 18 declared natural hazard events and more than 120,000 natural hazard claims costing about A$2 billion of roughly A$10 billion in total claims spending, exceeding its allowance by A$254 million.

Shareholders receive a 52 cent fully franked final dividend, taking the FY26 total to 69 cents, plus a 10 cent special dividend; an A$400 million buy-back is complete and up to A$250 million more is planned for FY27.
A multi-year aggregate reinsurance cover took effect on June 30, 2026, and the review cites more than 20 generative AI initiatives and a customer net promoter score of +11.7 versus +9.1.

Chair Duncan West said chief executive Steve Johnston took medical leave during the year and CFO Jeremy Robson acted as CEO, while a July report said ASIC's review of insurers' claims handling put Suncorp under regulatory scrutiny.
why_it_matters: Suncorp is one of Australia's largest home and motor insurers, so its annual review is a read-through for household premiums, natural hazard costs and shareholder returns. The year shows how an insurer can exceed its hazard allowance by a large amount and still deliver a profit and a higher payout, and how regulatory attention on claims handling sits alongside strong financial results.
